The manual is written from the guides kept beside the code: the [administrator guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/ADMIN-GUIDE.md), the [user guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/USER-GUIDE.md), the [deployment guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md), and [data in and out](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/DATA.md). Those go deeper into settings and file formats. What changed in each release is in the [changelog](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The screenshots show a demonstration organization with made-up clients. Your Atlas shows your own logo and colour.

**Atlas** The application. One service that serves the web pages and the API, runs scheduled jobs (syncs, checks, backups, alerts), and holds the vault key while it runs. **PostgreSQL** The database. Every client, asset, document, password and log entry is stored here. Passwords and other secrets are encrypted before they reach it. **Web proxy** Caddy on Linux installs. It serves Atlas over HTTPS and keeps its certificate up to date. **The master key** A key kept outside the database. It protects the vault key and every backup. Without it, encrypted data can't be read, so the person who runs the server keeps a copy offline. **The updater** A small helper on Linux installs. It installs new releases and carries out restarts and repairs when an administrator asks from the web page.

Every client you support gets a workspace. Its tabs are the same for every client: **Overview** The client at a glance: primary contact, hours, maintenance window, asset counts, warranty, device health, security, trackers, tickets and recent activity. **Assets** Servers, workstations, firewalls, switches, domains, SSL certificates, licences and anything else, each in a layout with its own fields. **Documents** Runbooks, procedures and notes for this client. **Passwords** The client's vault: logins, secure notes, one-time codes and BitLocker keys. **Contacts** and **Locations** The people you deal with and the sites you visit. **Checklists** Onboarding, offboarding and maintenance procedures worked through step by step. **Map** How the client's assets, passwords, documents, contacts and locations link together. **Activity** Every change, by whom and when. **Trackers** Domain and SSL certificate expiry for the client's websites.

You can type everything in, but most teams start by bringing it in: **Hudu** companies, layouts, assets, articles, passwords, processes and relations import in one run, and running it again updates rather than duplicates. **Spreadsheets** (CSV) bring in clients, contacts, locations, assets and passwords. **ConnectWise RMM** keeps devices, their health and their tickets up to date every hour. **Microsoft 365** turns each client's tenant into contacts, licences and domains. **Vendors** fill in warranty dates for Dell, Lenovo and HP devices, and domain registries and websites fill in expiry dates for domains and certificates. Chapter 12, [Data and integrations](integrations.html), explains each one.

Atlas decides everything by role and by client. A technician sees only the clients they have been given, and a client they can't open looks the same as one that doesn't exist. Passwords need a higher level of access than documentation. Client accounts see only their own organization. [Getting started](getting-started.html#what-you-can-do-depends-on-your-role) has the full table.

s: Sign in for the first time
t: Your administrator gives you the Atlas address, your email, and a temporary password. Open the Atlas address in your browser and sign in with your email and the temporary password. Choose your own password. It must be at least 12 characters; a few unrelated words work well. Set up two-step verification. Staff can't do anything else until it's on. Scan the QR code with an authenticator app (Microsoft Authenticator, Google Authenticator, 1Password and so on) and enter the six-digit code, or add a passkey instead. Save your recovery codes. They are shown once. Each one gets you in once if you lose your phone. Keep them somewhere other than Atlas. At the second step you can tick **Remember this browser for 30 days** so your own computer doesn't ask for a code every time. Only do this on a device that is yours. Passkeys A passkey is Windows Hello, Touch ID, your phone, or a security key. Add one under **Profile & sign-in → Passkeys** (open the account menu with your initials in the top-right header). After that, **Sign in with a passkey** on the sign-in page signs you in without typing a password, and can't be phished. Signing in with Microsoft or your identity provider If your company has set it up, the sign-in page shows **Sign in with Microsoft** or **Sign in with** your provider's name. Your account must already exist in Atlas. The first time you use it, an administrator confirms that the Microsoft or provider account is really yours, and until they do, Atlas asks you to wait. Forgot your password Choose **Forgot your password?** on the sign-in page. The link in the email works once, for an hour. If you have also lost your phone and recovery codes, an administrator can reset your sign-in.

Atlas is organized into five areas. Each area has a handful of pages. **Overview** Dashboard, Expirations, Reports Everyone **Clients** Client directory and client workspaces Everyone **Documentation** Assets, Knowledge base, Checklists Everyone; the knowledge base and checklists are for staff **Password Vault** Passwords, My vault, Password health, Send; Password rotation and BitLocker collector for administrators Staff **Administration** People and security, data, system, and settings pages Administrators Your account menu, with your initials, is in the top-right header. It has **Profile & sign-in**, light and dark appearance, and **Sign out**. Search everything with Ctrl+K Press **Ctrl+K** (or **⌘K** on a Mac) anywhere in Atlas, or click **Search** in the header. Type a client, an asset name, an IP address, a serial number, a contact, or words from a document. Use the arrow keys and **Enter** to open a result, or **Esc** to close. Results only include what you have access to. Navigation and workspace tabs Atlas uses a single sidebar for **Overview**, **Clients**, **Documentation**, **Password Vault**, and **Administration**. Page links appear in the current workspace. Where the menu doesn't list them (on a phone, with the sidebar collapsed, or in the top menu style), they appear as tabs along the top of the page. **Administration** has many pages, so its tabs show the section you're in, such as People and security, and **More** lists the rest under their headings. The client directory stays in **Clients**, global search, and the client switcher in the header rather than filling a second sidebar. Choose **Collapse sidebar** at the bottom of the sidebar to make more space for tables. **Expand sidebar** restores labels. Atlas remembers this choice in your browser. On phones, choose **Open navigation** in the header; Escape closes the menu and returns focus to its trigger. Favourites and the dashboard Click the star beside a client, asset or document to add it to the **Favorites** card on your dashboard. Choose **Customize** on the dashboard to show, hide and reorder its cards. Your layout is yours alone. **Reset to default** puts the standard layout back. Light and dark Choose the appearance in the account menu. Atlas remembers it per browser.

After an update with new features, your dashboard shows a **Welcome** card. **See what's new** opens a page describing each new part in plain words, with a link to try it. Opening the page, or choosing **Dismiss**, puts the card away for you; the page stays under **What's new** in the account menu (your initials, top right) to come back to.

s: What you can do depends on your role
t: Everyone in Atlas has one role, plus an access level for each client. **Owner** The person responsible for Atlas Every client, including passwords Everything, including other owners and vault policies **Administration** Service managers, senior technicians Every client, including passwords People, settings, imports, system **Technician** Your technicians The clients they're given, up to editing passwords None **Read-only technician** Trainees, auditors The clients they're given, read-only None **Client editor** A client's own staff who keep their documentation Their own organization, can edit None **Client viewer** A client's own staff Their own organization, read-only None For each client, a person's access is one of **No access**, **Read**, **Edit**, or **Edit + passwords**. Only **Edit + passwords** shows the client's vault. Your access to a client is shown under its name. A client you have no access to looks exactly like one that doesn't exist, on purpose. Ask an administrator to give you access under **Admin → People & access** or through a group.

**Profile & sign-in** is where you manage your own security: **Change password.** Changing it signs out your other devices. **Two-step verification**, **Authenticator app**, **Passkeys** and **Recovery codes.** Add a second method so losing your phone doesn't lock you out. **Where you're signed in.** Every browser session, with **Sign out** for each one you don't recognize. **Remembered browsers.** Forget any browser that no longer needs to skip the code. **Signed-in apps** and **Desktop apps.** The browser extension and Atlas for Windows, with **Sign out** for each. **Email notifications.** Tick **Email me about expirations** for alerts when certificates, domains, licences, warranties, password rotations and document reviews come due, plus a Monday digest.

**Tab** from the top of any page reaches **Skip to content** first. **Ctrl+K** opens search anywhere. **Esc** closes dialogs and menus, and focus returns to where you were. Every screen is tested against WCAG 2.2 AA in light and dark, and at phone width.

**Clients → All clients** lists every client you can open, with its status, your access, and when it last changed. Type in **Search clients** to filter, or choose **All**, **Active**, **Prospect** or **Inactive**. In the rail menu style, the **Go to** list in the Clients panel jumps straight to any client. Add a client You need edit access to every client to add one. Administrators always have it. Choose **Add client** on the client list. Enter the **Client name**, and choose its **Type** and **Status**. Optionally fill in **Hours of operation** and **Maintenance window**. They show on the client's overview, where technicians look before scheduling work. Tick **Require a reason to view passwords** if this client wants every password reveal explained. See [Passwords](passwords.html#reveal-and-copy-a-password). Choose **Save**. Importing from Hudu or a spreadsheet, or syncing ConnectWise RMM companies, creates clients for you. An imported company is matched to an existing client with the same name rather than creating a second one. See [Data and integrations](integrations.html).

Opening a client shows: **The header:** the client's name and type, your access, the star to add it to your favourites, and for staff the client's health score (see [Client health](#client-health)). **Review pack**, **Export**, **Edit client**, and for administrators **Delete**, are on the right. **Review pack** downloads this client's quarterly business review as one PDF (see [Client review pack](#client-review-pack)). **The quick note:** a short note at the top of every page for this client, for the thing everyone should know before they touch anything. **The tabs:** **Overview**, **Assets**, **Documents**, **Passwords**, **Contacts**, **Locations**, **Checklists**, **Licenses**, **Map** and **Activity**. Counts appear for the sections that provide them. The **Trackers** row underneath has **Domain Tracker** and **SSL Tracker**. A tracker count turns amber when something needs attention. Hide tabs you don't use Choose **Choose which sections show** (the sliders at the right of the tabs) and untick the sections you don't need. This only changes your own view; other people still see every tab. Client health Every client has a health score from 0 to 100, beside its name, with a word for how it's doing: **Healthy:** 90 and over. **Good:** 75 to 89. **Needs attention:** 60 to 74. **At risk:** under 60. An arrow shows how far it has moved in the last 30 days. The score is made of four parts, weighted by how much they matter: **Security** 30% Passwords without issues, endpoint protection running, and disks encrypted (where the BitLocker collector reports). **Endpoints** 25% Devices online, and devices that checked in with the RMM on time. **Documentation** 25% A primary contact, a location, assets, and documents on record, and documents reviewed by their review date. **Renewals** 20% Domains, SSL certificates, warranties and subscriptions in date. An expired item counts fully against it; one due soon counts half. A part with nothing to measure, such as a client with no RMM devices, is left out and the others count for more. It is never assumed to be healthy. Choose the score to see each part and **What would raise it most**: each thing pulling the score down, with how many points fixing it would add, linked to where you fix it. Atlas works the scores out every hour with the owner's view, so everyone on staff sees the same number. It keeps one score per client per day, for the trend. Scores are for staff only; client accounts don't see them. The dashboard's **Client health** card lists every client you can open, lowest first, with its trend; **Customize** moves or hides it. The client list has a **Health** column. The **Executive summary** report includes each client's score and its parts, and the [Client review pack](#client-review-pack) shows the score on its cover.

The overview is the client at a glance. Scroll down for the detail. **Facts** Primary contact, phone, hours of operation and maintenance window. **Assets** How many assets the client has in each layout. Choose one to open the list. **Contact and location** The primary contact's details and the primary location's address. **Asset warranty** Hardware by when its warranty ends: expired, ending soon, active, unknown. **RMM health** From ConnectWise RMM: devices online, stale agents, and endpoint protection. **Security and compliance** From ConnectWise: patch compliance, backup and DR readiness, vulnerabilities and MDR incidents. A part the client doesn't use says *Not available*. **Domain and SSL expiry** What is expired or expiring among the client's domains and certificates. **Asset statistics** Servers, workstations, network devices, printers and phones, and a chart of operating systems that marks the ones out of support. **Tickets** and **Ticket details** Tickets opened and closed per day, and the open tickets that have gone longest without an update. **Installed software** Applications reported by ConnectWise RMM across the client's devices. **Recently updated documents** and **Recent activity** What changed lately, and who changed it. Several changes in a row by one person show as one line. Cards that rely on ConnectWise only appear once the client is linked to a ConnectWise company. Chapter 6, [Monitoring and alerts](monitoring.html), explains each card in detail.

The quick note is for one or two lines everyone must see: "Practice management runs on-prem, never reboot the server before 6 PM", or "New firewall going in next week." Choose **Edit** on the note to change it. **History** shows every earlier version, lets you compare two, and restore one.

The **Contacts** and **Locations** tabs list the people and sites for this client. **Add contact** or **Add location** opens a form. Tick **Primary contact** or **Primary location** to show it on the overview. A contact's email and phone numbers are links, so you can call or write from the page. Link a contact or location to the assets and documents it relates to from the item's **Related** section. See [Documentation](documentation.html#link-related-items).

The **Map** tab draws how the client's assets, passwords, documents, contacts and locations link together, with the same links as a list below for keyboard and screen-reader use. It's built from the links you make under **Related** on each item.

Open **Licenses** to track software subscriptions, purchased seats, assigned people or devices, per-seat costs, billing cycles, and renewal dates. Choose **Add subscription**, enter one assignment per line, and save. Assignment counts cannot exceed purchased seats. Renewals within 30 days and past renewal dates receive a badge; this page does not send renewal emails. Keep activation keys and passwords in the vault. For linked Microsoft 365 tenants, **Microsoft 365** reads subscriptions, seat availability, and users through the saved **GDAP** partner connection. Choose a subscription to inspect assignments. Atlas administrators can assign an available license to a user or remove a direct assignment after confirming the named user and product. Group-assigned licenses must be changed through Microsoft Entra group membership. Microsoft consent and the partner user's customer roles also apply; see [Data and integrations](integrations.html#microsoft-365). Microsoft seat counts and assignments remain authoritative in Microsoft. Purchases, reseller pricing, billing terms, and renewal dates are managed with your reseller. **Other software subscriptions** tracks other purchases manually and does not change vendor subscriptions. Read-only client access can view records; editing manual tracking requires client edit access. Manual changes appear in client activity and client exports.

Open **Overview → Reports** for reporting across clients, or a client's **Reports** tab for that workspace. The built-in reports are: Client review pack Executive summary Security posture Cyber insurance readiness Service review Asset inventory License utilization Savings finder Upcoming renewals Domains & SSL Documentation health Endpoint health Software & sign-ins Microsoft 365 accounts Microsoft 365 usage Choose a report and up to 25 clients, set the report title and any lookahead, and choose **Run report**. The report captures current records; it does not infer historical activity or missing health data. Source timestamps and coverage notices explain what was available. Microsoft seat inventory is read only through the linked GDAP connection. Microsoft reseller costs and renewal dates are not supplied by that inventory. A report opens with its figures across the top, then every section of it, one after another. Press **Needs review** (or tick **Needs review only**) to show just the flagged rows, and use the search box to search the whole report. Each section's **CSV** exports its matching rows, up to the 10,000-row generation limit; **PDF** exports the whole report, with capture details and data coverage. The page shows the first 500 rows of a section; the CSV has them all. **Save template** stores reusable settings privately in your account. **Templates** lets you load, update, copy, or delete those settings. **History** lists your recent snapshots; opening a snapshot preserves its original contents, while **Refresh report** creates a new capture. Every view and download checks current access to all included clients. Deleting a client removes any report or template containing that client. Report generation, template changes, exports, and deletions appear in the security log. **Security posture** shows, for each client, passwords with problems (breached, weak, reused, overdue, expired, or unchanged for a year), devices that are offline or unprotected, BitLocker encryption reported by the collector, and the last result of automatic password rotation. Password names appear only for clients whose passwords you can open, and only administrators see rotation. Passwords, usernames, notes, and recovery keys are never included. **Savings finder** shows what each client pays for and doesn't use, priced per month: **Unused seats:** seats bought but not assigned. A subscription tracked under **Licenses** counts only when its assignments are recorded, so nothing is guessed; a notice lists the ones without assignments. **Licenses on blocked accounts:** Microsoft 365 licenses held by accounts whose sign-in is blocked, usually people who have left. Remove the licenses, or convert the mailbox to a shared mailbox, which needs no license under 50 GB. **Renewals:** tracked subscriptions renewing within the window you choose, with what each renewal costs, how many seats go unused, and what cutting them saves before it renews. The summary totals each client's monthly and yearly waste, in each currency separately. Microsoft 365 seats come live through GDAP (choose **Include Microsoft 365 inventory through GDAP**). GDAP doesn't give prices, so a Microsoft seat is priced from a tracked subscription of the same name when you have one. Otherwise it's estimated at Microsoft's published list price in US dollars, marked "(list)", and products Atlas has no price for show as "Not priced". A product Microsoft reports is counted from Microsoft's live assignments, never twice. **Microsoft 365 accounts** lists every account in each client's linked tenant: enabled or blocked, member or guest, how many licenses it holds, and its usage location. Blocked accounts that still hold licenses, and licensed accounts with no usage location, are flagged. **Microsoft 365 usage** shows who uses Microsoft 365 and how, over the last 30 to 180 days (Microsoft keeps 180): each licensed account's last activity in email, Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint, flagging accounts with none, then a section each for Exchange email, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and the Microsoft 365 apps. It reads Microsoft's usage reports, which need the **Reports.Read.All** permission and a GDAP role that can read reports (see *Microsoft 365 with GDAP* in the administrator's guide). If a tenant hides names in its reports, the report says how to show them. **Cyber insurance readiness** answers the questions cyber insurers ask, for each client, from what Atlas holds. Each answer is **Yes**, **Partly**, **No** or **Not evidenced**, with the evidence and where it came from: MFA for email and remote access Not tracked in Atlas: confirm it in Microsoft Entra Endpoint protection on every device ConnectWise RMM Laptops and workstations encrypted The BitLocker collector Operating systems still supported Device operating systems on assets Devices managed and up to date RMM check-ins (patch levels are in the RMM) Backups in place and restore-tested in 12 months **Backups** assets and their **Last restore test** Administrator accounts limited Global Administrators of the synced Microsoft 365 tenant (fewer than five) Local administrator passwords rotated Automatic password rotation (administrators only) Stored passwords free of breaches and reuse Password health Email protected against spoofing Each **Domains** asset's DMARC record, looked up when the report runs, and the filtering service on **Email** assets Incident response plan A document titled as one Business continuity or disaster recovery plan A document titled as one Security awareness training Not tracked in Atlas **Readiness summary** gives each client's readiness: Yes counts fully and Partly half, out of the questions Atlas could answer. **Gaps to close before renewal** lists every answer that isn't Yes, refusals first, each with what to do. **Not evidenced** means Atlas holds no proof either way, so answer it from your own records rather than as a Yes. A DMARC lookup that fails is a notice, never "no record". **Domains & SSL** lists each client's domains and SSL certificates with their registrar or issuer, expiry date, days left, and the result of the latest automatic check, soonest first. A summary counts what has expired, what expires within the chosen window, and failed checks. Records the trackers haven't checked yet show the dates as entered. **Software & sign-ins** reads the inventory the ConnectWise RMM sync saves. It lists every application installed on each client's devices, with versions, how many devices have it, and the same flags as the client's Software tab: end of life, no license recorded, or more installs than licensed seats. It also lists the accounts that sign in to each device, with the matching contact. Devices that haven't reported an inventory are counted in the report's notices rather than treated as having nothing installed. **Service review** looks back over a period you choose (the last 30 days to a year): tickets opened and closed, tickets still open, checklists completed, documentation updated, assets added, and every change recorded in Atlas, with each client's device health at the start of the period against now. It suits a monthly or quarterly review with the client. Password changes are counted only for clients whose passwords you can open, and are never listed. For **Asset inventory**, **Asset fields** adds up to 12 fields from your asset layouts as extra columns, such as serial number, model, warranty date, or IP address. Long text fields are never included, because they often hold notes and configuration. A field removed from its layout since a template was saved is left out, with a notice. PDF exports carry your organization's look from **Administration → Theme**: the logo (PNG or JPEG; an SVG logo shows your brand name instead), the brand name, and the accent colour. The first page summarizes the report: how many clients and rows it covers, how many rows need review, and any notices. It also charts what needs review in each section, the spread of status columns (online, protection, encryption, status), and due or expiry dates by month. When you have run the same report for the same clients before, **Compare with** shows what changed since the most recent earlier run. New rows are marked **New**, changed values are highlighted with the previous value beneath, and rows that have gone are listed under **removed since**. **Changes only** hides everything else. Values that move on every run, such as check-in times or days left, don't count as changes. Client review pack The **Client review pack** is a business review for one client in a single PDF, ready to send before a quarterly meeting. It is made of four reports, run together: **Executive summary**, **Security posture**, **Service review** and **Upcoming renewals**. Its period looks back for the service review and ahead for renewals: a quarter by default, or anything from 30 days to a year. The fastest way to make one is **Review pack** in the client's header: it captures the last quarter and downloads the PDF in one click. You can also choose **Client review pack** under Reports, pick the client and period, and choose **Run report**, then **Review pack PDF**. The PDF opens with a cover page in your organization's look. It shows the client, the period, how much of each report needs review, and the contents with page numbers. Each report follows on its own pages, with its charts, and one-client summaries shown as figures rather than a one-row table. On screen, **Report section** groups the sections under the report each belongs to. The pack leaves out Atlas's internal change log; the service review still counts the changes made. Like any single-client report, a review pack can be compared with the last one, shared with the client by link (the client can download all of it as one PDF), or scheduled, for example every quarter on the 1st. Scheduled reports To have a report emailed regularly, set it up (report type, clients, and any options), then choose **Schedule**. Choose: how often it runs: every day, week, month, or quarter (quarters start in January, April, July, and October); the day and the hour, in the server's time zone; who receives it: up to 20 addresses, staff or client contacts. Each time it runs, Atlas captures a fresh snapshot with your access at that moment and keeps it in your **History**, so **Compare with** works on it. Then it emails each recipient a summary, with the whole report attached as a PDF in your organization's look. For a report about one client, it can also include a 30-day link the client can open without an account. The **Scheduled** tab lists your schedules, when each runs next, and how the last delivery went, including any addresses that refused it. **Deliveries** lists every email a schedule sent or tried to send, recipient by recipient, with the reason any was refused. Send one again to its recipient with the resend button: it sends the same snapshot, without running the report again, while that snapshot is still in your history. **Send now** sends one straight away without moving its regular time. **Pause** stops it until you resume it. Schedules are private to the person who made them. A schedule stops if its owner can no longer sign in, and deleting a client removes the schedules that report on it. Email must be set up under **Administration → Email & alerts**. Sharing a report with the client A report run for a single client can be shared with that client by link. Choose **Share**, pick how long the link works (7, 30, or 90 days; report links always expire), and choose **Create link**; the link is copied for you. Whoever has the link sees that snapshot, every section as it was captured, and can download the whole report or one section as a PDF, without an account. The page names your organization and the client, never the person who ran the report. The dialog shows how often each link was opened, and **Revoke** stops a link at once. Deleting the report or the client stops its links too. Only the person who ran the report can share it, and only with edit access to the client. Making and revoking links appear in the security log. **Send** decides which runs are emailed, so a schedule can work as an alert: **Every time** sends every run. **Only when something needs review** sends only runs with flagged rows. **Only when something new needs review** sends only when something needs review that didn't in the last report sent. That email lists just the new items. For example, **Security posture**, every day, **only when something new needs review**, tells you the morning after a password turns up in a breach or a device loses its protection, and stays quiet otherwise. **Domains & SSL** set up the same way warns as each certificate or domain starts to expire. Runs that send nothing aren't kept in your history, and the schedule shows **Nothing to send**. **Send now** always sends.

**Export** downloads a zip of everything you can see for the client: `client.json`, with the client, contacts, locations, assets and their fields, documents, manually tracked subscriptions, and links. The documents as plain text. The attached files. Administrators can tick **Include decrypted passwords**. Atlas asks for your password again first, and every password exported is logged. Keep such an export encrypted, and delete it when you're done.

**Edit client** changes the name, type, status, hours, maintenance window and the reason requirement. **Delete** (administrators only) removes the client and everything in it. You must type the client's name exactly. The deletion is recorded in the security log. It can't be undone except by restoring a backup. A deleted client's assets, documents, passwords and history are gone. If you only stopped working with them, set the status to **Inactive** instead.

An asset is anything you look after: a server, a workstation, a firewall, a switch, a domain name, an SSL certificate, a software licence. Each asset uses a **layout** that decides its fields. Atlas comes with layouts such as Configurations, Endpoints, Networks, Domains, SSL certificates and Licenses, and administrators can add their own. **Docs → Assets** lists assets across every client you can see. A client's **Assets** tab lists just theirs, grouped by layout. Add an asset Open the client and go to its **Assets** tab, then choose **Add asset**. Pick the layout. Fill in the fields. Atlas checks them as you save: an IP address, date, email address or web address in the wrong format is pointed out before anything is saved. Choose **Save**. Smart paste Rather than typing a computer's details, let it tell you: On the computer, run one of these: **Windows:** `ipconfig /all`, `systeminfo` or, in PowerShell, `Get-ComputerInfo`. Several can be pasted together. **Mac:** `system_profiler SPHardwareDataType`. **Linux:** `hostnamectl`. Copy what it prints. In the new asset, choose **Smart paste** and paste it. Or simply paste it into the **Name** box: Atlas recognises it and opens Smart paste for you. Atlas shows what it found: the name, hostname, IP address (the network card with a gateway comes first), MAC address, manufacturer, model, serial number, operating system and type (server, laptop or workstation). Empty fields are ticked to fill. A field that already holds something different shows what it would replace, and stays unticked. Choose **Fill in**, check the fields, then save. The text is read in your browser and isn't sent or kept. It works with any layout that has fields with these names, not only Configurations. Devices from ConnectWise RMM and tenants from Microsoft 365 arrive as assets on their own; you don't need to add them by hand. Fields filled by a sync are kept up to date by the sync, and fields you add yourself are left alone. An asset's page An asset's page shows its **Details** (every field in its layout), **Notes** and **Activity**. Down the right are: **BitLocker**, for Windows machines that report through the BitLocker collector or ConnectWise RMM. See [Passwords](passwords.html#bitlocker-recovery-keys). **Related**, the passwords, documents, contacts and locations linked to it. **Files**, anything attached. **Version history**, every saved version. The buttons at the top are **QR label**, **Check warranty** (for hardware with a serial number), **Archive** and **Edit**. Archive instead of deleting **Archive** takes an asset out of lists and counts without losing it. **Show archived** on the assets list shows them, and **Restore** on an archived asset brings it back. Assets that a ConnectWise RMM sync no longer finds are archived for you. Warranty dates For Dell, Lenovo and HP hardware with a serial number, Atlas looks up the warranty end date from the vendor's public warranty check when the asset is saved, and during each ConnectWise RMM sync. **Check warranty** looks it up again now. A date someone typed in is never replaced. QR labels Choose **QR label** on an asset, or **QR labels** on a client's Assets tab for everything shown. Pick a label size and print. Scanning a label with a phone opens that asset in Atlas after signing in. The label itself shows only the name, the client and the serial number, so nothing sensitive is printed.

Documents are runbooks, procedures, how-tos and notes. They live in a client's **Documents** tab, or in the MSP **Knowledge base** for procedures that apply to every client. Write a document Choose **New document**, on a client's Documents tab or in **Docs → Knowledge base**. Give it a **Title**, and choose a **Folder** if you use them. Write it. The editor has headings, bulleted and numbered lists, checklists, tables, code blocks and links. Set its **Status**: **Current**, **Needs review** or **Draft**. Optionally set **Review by**. Atlas reminds you on the Expirations page when the date comes, so procedures don't quietly go out of date. Choose **Save**. Still accurate? Verify it When you've checked a document and it's still right, choose **Verify**. The document shows **Verified 12 days ago by Alex**, so the next person knows it can be trusted. **Verifying isn't an edit:** the version and "last updated" stay as they were. **Needs review clears:** a document marked **Needs review** goes back to **Current**. **The review comes round again:** if it has a **Review by** date, that date moves six months ahead, so the reminder repeats. **Stale documents are marked:** one that hasn't been verified or edited for six months shows **Not verified**, or **Last verified** in amber. The documentation health report lists them too. The knowledge base **Docs → Knowledge base** is your team's own library: procedures, standards and how-tos that aren't about one client. Client accounts never see it. **New folder** keeps it organized. **Template library** offers ready-made runbooks to start from. They go into a Runbooks folder, and you edit them like any other document. Share a document with a link **Share** on a document makes a link anyone can open without signing in, for a how-to you want to send to a client's staff. They see that one document, always as it is now, and nothing else in Atlas. Choose how long the link works. Atlas shows how often it has been opened. **Revoke** stops the link working at once. Anyone with the link can read the document. Don't share one that contains passwords or anything about another client.

Checklists are procedures you work through step by step: onboarding a new user, decommissioning a laptop, patching a server. A checklist is the reusable template; a **run** is one time you work through it for a client. Make a checklist Go to **Docs → Checklists** and choose **New checklist**, or **Template library** to start from one of 13 ready-made checklists (client and user onboarding and offboarding, endpoint setup and decommission, server patching, backup verification, Microsoft 365 setup, firewall change, password rotation, incident response, SSL and domain renewal). Give it a **Title** and choose **Add a step** for each step. Make it available to every client, or to one. Steps are copied into each run when it starts, so changing a checklist later doesn't change work already under way. Run a checklist for a client On the client's **Checklists** tab, choose **Start a checklist**. Pick the **Checklist** (or write a one-off list of **Steps**), and choose who to **Assign to**. Tick each step as you do it. Atlas records who ticked it and when. **Add a note** records what you found. Set a **Due** date if it has one. An overdue run is marked. **Markdown** downloads the run as a text file, and **Print or PDF** gives you a printed record for the client.

Every asset, document, password, contact and location has a **Related** section. Choose **Link** to connect it to others: the firewall to its runbook, its admin password and the site it's in. Links work both ways, so the runbook shows the firewall too, and the client's **Map** tab draws them all.

Drag files onto the **Files** section of any asset or document to attach them, or choose **Upload**. Images that pass a content check show inline; other files download. Files are stored outside the web server's reach under random names.

Every save keeps the previous version. **Version history** lists every version with who saved it and when. **Compare** shows what changed between two versions, line by line, and **Restore version** puts an old one back as a new version. If someone else saved while you were editing, Atlas tells you instead of overwriting their work. Copy your changes, reload, and apply them again.

Administrators manage layouts under **Admin → Asset layouts**. A layout has a name, an icon and fields. Each field has a type: **Text**, **Long text**, **Number**, **Date**, **Choice**, **Multiple choice**, **Yes / no**, **Web address**, **Email**, **Phone**, or **IP address or subnet**. A date field can be ticked as an **Expiry date**, which puts it on the Expirations page and in expiry alerts.

Imports and syncs sometimes create the same thing twice. **Admin → Duplicates** lists assets, contacts and locations with the same name in the same client, and clients with the same name. Choose the record to keep and merge the rest into it: blank fields are filled in, links and files move over, and merged assets are archived so they can be restored.

**Vault → Passwords** lists every password you can open. A client's **Passwords** tab lists just theirs, with **Folders** down the side. On each row you can copy the username, the password or the one-time code without opening the entry. The star keeps a password at the top of the list. Tick several entries to archive or restore them together, change how often they rotate, or start or stop sharing them with the client.

The eye shows the password. **Copy password** puts it on the clipboard, and Atlas clears the clipboard after 30 seconds. The six-digit one-time code for accounts with an authenticator updates live. **Copy one-time code** copies it. Some clients require a reason first. Atlas asks *Why do you need this password?* and keeps your answer with the record of the reveal. A ticket number is a good reason. Every reveal, copy, change and share appears under **Access history** on the entry, and in **Admin → Security log → Vault access**.

On the client's **Passwords** tab, choose **Add password**. Choose the **Type**: a login, a secure note, or a BitLocker recovery key. Fill in the **Name**, username, password and **Website or address**. The address is what the browser extension matches against. Use the generator for a random password or a passphrase. **Presets** remember the lengths and character sets your team uses. If the account has two-step sign-in, paste its **Authenticator setup key (TOTP)** so Atlas can show the one-time code. Optionally set **Rotate every** (how often it should change), **Account expires**, a **Folder**, **Notes (encrypted)**, extra fields with **Add a field**, and the assets it belongs to under **Linked assets**. Choose **Save**. Atlas warns you when a password is weak or already used elsewhere.

A password in the **Wi-Fi** category shows its username as the **Network name**, and has a **Join this network** card underneath: a code that phones scan with their camera to join without typing the password. Choose **Show the code**. The password is revealed the usual way: it's recorded in the access history, and a reason is asked for where the client requires one. The code appears beside the network's details. Change the **Security** setting for a WEP or open network, and tick **Hidden network** for one that doesn't broadcast its name, so phones know to look for it. **Print** prints a card on its own, with the network name, the code and (unless you untick it) the password underneath, ready to frame for a waiting room. **PNG** downloads the code as a picture. Like a shown password, the code hides again after a minute.

s: Change a password and its history
t: Edit the entry and enter the new password. The old one moves to **Previous passwords**, with when it changed, so you can still find it if the change didn't take everywhere. If the entry has **Rotate every** set, it appears on the Expirations page when the change is due, and in expiry alerts.

s: Restrict an entry to named people
t: Some passwords should only be open to a few people: a domain admin, a payroll login. Edit the entry and tick **Restricted**, then tick the groups and people under **Who can use it**. Everyone else can't see the entry exists. By default, administrators still see restricted entries. The owner can change that in **Vault policies**, so restricted means only the people listed. See [People and access](people-and-access.html#vault-policies).

s: Share with the client's own staff
t: Tick **Share with the client's own accounts** on an entry so the client's own contacts can see it when they sign in to Atlas, read-only. Each view is recorded for you.

For someone outside Atlas, send a link instead of pasting a password into email or chat. **Quick share** makes a link that opens once, within 24 hours, and copies it. **More options** lets you choose how many times it **Can be opened** and when it **Expires after**. The password is encrypted in your browser, and the key is only in the part of the link after the `#`, which never reaches the server. Send the link through a different channel from the username. **Share links** on the entry lists the links you've made, and you can revoke any of them.

s: Send text or a file once
t: **Vault → Send** is for anything else you need to hand over once: a licence key, a config file, instructions. Choose **New Send**, then text or a file. Give it a **Name** (only you see it), choose how many times it **Can be opened** and when it **Expires after**. Copy the **Send link** and give it to the recipient. Like share links, it's encrypted in your browser before it's uploaded, and Atlas never has the key. Administrators can tick **Show everyone's Sends** to see what's outstanding.

**Vault → My vault** is a private place for logins and notes that are yours alone: your own vendor portal account, your payroll login, a door code. **Only you can see it.** Not administrators, not the owner. It isn't attached to any client and doesn't appear in search, reports, password health, exports or the audit log. **Add** a login or a secure note. The generator and one-time codes work the same as in a client's vault. **In the browser extension,** your own logins are offered on matching sites, marked *My vault*. **Deleting is permanent.** There is no archive and no history. **Move to a client** turns an entry that belongs to the team into one of a client's passwords. It leaves your vault and can't be moved back. **Export** downloads your vault as a CSV file in the layout Bitwarden uses. Atlas asks for your password first. The file holds every password in plain text, so import it and delete it. Nobody can open your personal vault after your account is closed. Move what the company needs to its client, and export the rest, before you go. The owner can turn personal vaults off for everyone in Vault policies. Nothing is deleted, and everything comes back if they're turned on again.

**Vault → Password health** reports weak, reused, overdue, expired, old and breached passwords across the clients you can open, with a score for each client, lowest first. Filter by problem, open an entry to fix it, or export the list as CSV. Nothing on the page shows a password. **Breached** passwords are found with Have I Been Pwned. Only the first five characters of a scrambled (SHA-1) fingerprint leave the server, and Atlas stores only a count. An administrator can untick **Check passwords against known breaches** on the same page for servers without internet access.

BitLocker keys are kept as their own type of entry, and the 48-digit key is checked for typos as you type it. They arrive in three ways: **By hand:** **Add password**, then the BitLocker type. **The BitLocker collector:** a script your RMM runs on each Windows machine reads its BitLocker status and recovery keys and sends them to Atlas. See [Data and integrations](integrations.html#bitlocker-collector). **ConnectWise RMM:** if your keys are already in a device custom field, the sync's **BitLocker keys** option saves them to the vault. A machine's asset page shows a **BitLocker** panel with each drive's protection, and its keys are under **Related**.

Administrators can have Atlas change local administrator and Active Directory service account passwords on a schedule, through ConnectWise RMM. The vault only changes after the device confirms the new password. See [Data and integrations](integrations.html#automatic-password-rotation).

The dashboard on **Home** puts it all on one page: totals across your clients, then the cards below, for every client you can see. Each client's overview has the same cards for that client alone. Choose any tile, slice or row to list the devices or items behind it.

**Home → Expirations** lists everything coming due, grouped by when: overdue, then the coming weeks. It includes: Asset date fields marked as expiry dates, such as certificate and domain expiry, licence renewals and warranties. Password rotations that are due. Documents whose **Review by** date has come. If something is missing, check that its layout's date field is ticked as an **Expiry date** (see [Asset layouts](documentation.html#asset-layouts)).

Atlas emails people who tick **Email me about expirations** on their account page: **An alert** the chosen number of days before each thing is due. **A weekly digest** on Monday mornings, listing everything overdue or due in the coming weeks. Administrators choose the alert days and the digest under **Admin → Email & alerts → Alerts and logs**. Email itself must be set up first, on the same page.

From ConnectWise RMM, for clients linked to a ConnectWise company. **Devices, Servers, Workstations, Offline servers** Counts across the synced devices. An offline server is marked. **Agent online** Devices online, offline, and unknown right now. **Stale agents** How long since each agent last checked in: current (under 7 days), stale, very stale (30 days or more), and never reported. **Endpoint protection** Whether the antivirus is running, not running, missing, or not reported. **Last 30 days** How each percentage has moved over the month. Administrators change when an agent counts as stale under **Admin → Monitoring → RMM health**.

Hardware assets by when their warranty ends: expired, expiring soon, active, and unknown. For Dell, Lenovo and HP devices with a serial number, Atlas looks the date up from the vendor's public warranty check, with no API keys to set up. A date someone typed in is never replaced. Under **Admin → Monitoring → Asset warranty**, administrators choose how many days count as expiring soon, and can untick **Look up warranties automatically**.

Each client's **Domain Tracker** and **SSL Tracker** tabs list its domains and certificates with their expiry dates. The **Domain and SSL expiry** card shows what is expired or expiring. **Domains** are re-checked with their registry weekly, and daily once they're within 60 days of expiring. **Certificates** are read from each website daily. **Check now** on a tracker tab checks straight away. The dates are saved on the asset, so they appear on Expirations and in alerts. Some registries don't publish an expiry date, and a certificate can only be read from a site Atlas can reach on port 443. For those, type the date on the asset. Under **Admin → Monitoring → Domain and SSL trackers**, administrators can turn the schedule off, and choose whether to **Add SSL certificates for domains** automatically when a domain's website serves a certificate the client has no asset for.

Servers, workstations, switches, network devices, printers and phones, and a chart of operating systems that marks the ones out of support. Choose a tile or a slice to list the devices. Administrators decide which asset layouts count as which kind of device under **Admin → Monitoring → Asset statistics**.

For clients linked to a ConnectWise company: **Patch compliance** for Windows and third-party software. **Backup and DR readiness.** **Vulnerabilities** by severity. **Security incidents (MDR)** that are open. A synced device's asset page has its own card with missing patches, backup jobs and vulnerabilities. Areas your ConnectWise partner account doesn't use show *Not available*.

When ticket sync is on, the **Tickets** card shows tickets opened and closed per day and a tile for each status, and **Ticket details** on each client's overview lists the open tickets that have gone longest without an update. Ticket numbers match the ConnectWise portal, and each one links to the ticket there. Tickets are read-only in Atlas.

Every client has an **Activity** tab, and the dashboard and overview have **Recent activity**: who created, changed, archived or linked what, and when. Several changes in a row by the same person to the same kind of thing show as one line ending "and N more".

The Atlas extension for Microsoft Edge and Google Chrome fills logins from the vault on the site you're on. Sign the extension in Click the Atlas button in the browser toolbar. Enter your Atlas address and choose **Sign in through Atlas**. Atlas opens in a new tab. Check it shows the same code as the extension, then choose **Allow**. You may be asked for your password. You never type a password into the extension itself. Fill a login On a sign-in page, click the Atlas button, or press **Alt+Shift+A**. Logins saved for that site are listed first, then logins elsewhere on the same domain, marked *Same domain*. Your own logins from My vault are marked *My vault*. Choose **Fill**. The username and password go into the page. On sites that ask for the username first, fill once for the username and again on the password page. Clients that require a reason ask for one first. Copy instead Search by name, username, address or client to copy a password, username or one-time code for any login you can use. The extension can't clear the clipboard after it closes, so prefer **Fill** when you can. Which logins match a site A login matches when its **Website or address** has the same host as the page, or the same domain, so a login saved for `login.example.com` is offered on `portal.example.com`. Addresses on shared hosting, such as `*.github.io`, and IP addresses only match exactly. An `https://` login is never offered on a plain `http://` page. Signing out Use **Sign out** in the extension, or **Signed-in apps** on your account page. The extension also signs itself out after 7 days unused, 30 days after signing in, and whenever your password changes or an administrator signs you out. For administrators: installing the extension `npm run build:extension` builds it. The unpacked extension goes to `apps/extension/dist`, and a zip to `apps/extension/package`. To try it, open `edge://extensions` or `chrome://extensions`, turn on developer mode, and **Load unpacked** with the `dist` folder. For your team, publish the zip privately in the Edge Add-ons or Chrome Web Store dashboard, or host it and force-install it with the `ExtensionInstallForcelist` group policy. It can only read and fill the tab you open it on, and it asks to reach one address: your Atlas. It stores the Atlas address, a session token and a signing key the browser won't let it export. No passwords, codes or lists of logins.

A small app in the notification area, for looking things up without opening a browser tab. Install it Open your account page in Atlas and find **Desktop apps**. Choose **Download** and run `AtlasForWindowsSetup.exe`. Windows may say it doesn't recognize the publisher, because the app isn't code-signed yet. Choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**. It installs for you only and doesn't need an administrator. The `.sha256` file beside each download in the GitHub release lets you check the file. Atlas for Windows refuses a certificate Windows doesn't trust, and has no way to override that. If your Atlas was installed at an IP address, install its certificate authority first. See [Keeping Atlas healthy](looking-after-atlas.html#the-certificate). Sign in Enter your Atlas address and choose **Sign in with your browser**. Your browser opens, you sign in as usual, and you approve the app. The app never sees your password. Search and copy Press **Ctrl+Shift+Space** anywhere in Windows, or click the Atlas icon in the notification area. Type. It searches the clients, assets, documents, contacts, locations and passwords you can see. With a password selected, **Enter** copies it. The buttons copy the username or the one-time code, or open the sign-in address. A copy is recorded like a reveal in the browser, asks for a reason where the client requires one, is kept out of Windows clipboard history, and is cleared from the clipboard after 30 seconds. Your personal vault isn't available in the app. On an item's page Under a password, asset or document, the app shows what it's linked to (open any of them with one click) and its files, which you save where you choose with **Save**; nothing is opened for you. A password also lists its earlier versions: show or copy one (recorded like any reveal), or, if you can edit the password, make it the current one again with **Restore**. A one-time code counts down the seconds until it changes. **Archived** at the top of the Passwords, Assets and Documents lists shows what was archived; an archived item opens read-only with **Restore**. Windows Hello and locking Where Windows Hello (fingerprint, face or PIN) is set up, the app asks for it before it shows or copies a password or one-time code. One check covers the next 5 minutes; you can make it every time, or 15 minutes, under **Windows Hello** in the account menu. The app also locks when the computer goes 15 minutes without keyboard or mouse use, hiding anything on screen until Windows Hello confirms it's you; choose 5, 15 or 30 minutes, an hour, or never, or choose **Lock now**. On a computer without Windows Hello the app doesn't ask and doesn't lock, since nothing could unlock it; set Windows Hello up under Windows Settings › Accounts › Sign-in options. Updates The app asks Atlas for a newer version when it starts and every six hours, and you can ask at any time with **Check for updates** in the account menu. When one is out, the app tells you once, shows **Install and restart** at the top of the window, and adds **Install version … and restart** to its tray menu. Choosing it downloads the setup program, checks it against the checksum published with the release, installs it over the old copy, and opens the app again; you stay signed in. Nothing installs until you choose to. If the download fails its checks, nothing is installed and the app says why, with a link to download it in your browser instead. Sign out **Sign out** in the app's menu, or **Desktop apps** on your account page. Use the account page if the computer is lost: it ends the app's session at once. For administrators: rolling it out Run `AtlasForWindowsSetup.exe /VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES` from your RMM as the signed-in person, not as SYSTEM, because it installs per person. **Sign out everywhere** on the People & access page, disabling an account, or resetting its sign-in also ends the app's session.

A client account sees only its own organization, and only what you give it: The documentation you've shared: assets, documents, contacts and locations. The passwords you've marked **Share with the client's own accounts**, read-only. Your logo, colour and welcome message. They never see the MSP knowledge base, other clients, your checklists, the vault for anything you haven't shared, or any administration page. They can't use the browser extension or Atlas for Windows.

Go to **Admin → People & access** and choose **Add person**. Enter their name and email. Choose the role: **Client viewer** to read their documentation. **Client editor** to also keep it up to date themselves. Under **Client access**, give them their own organization. Choose **Create account**. Atlas gives you a temporary password for them to change at first sign-in.

Open a password and tick **Share with the client's own accounts**. Their contacts can then see it when they sign in. To share several at once, tick them on the client's Passwords tab and change their client portal sharing together. Every view is recorded for you in the password's access history. If the client requires reasons, they're asked too. If you'd rather client viewers could see which passwords exist but not reveal them, the owner can tick **Don't let read-only accounts reveal passwords** in Vault policies.
**Admin → Theme** sets your logo, accent colour, and a welcome message that client accounts see at the top of their dashboard. Use it for how to reach your help desk.

If your IT provider gave you an account: **Sign in** at the address they gave you with your email and the temporary password, then choose your own password. **What you see** is your organization's documentation, your contacts and locations, and the passwords shared with you. **To view a password**, choose **Show password**. You may be asked for a reason, and each view is recorded for your provider. **To change something**, you need to be a *Client editor*. Otherwise, ask your provider.

The installer sets up Node.js 22, PostgreSQL 16 and Caddy on Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, or Debian 12, builds Atlas, and runs it as a systemd service. It installs the newest published release, so these commands never need a version number. The script prints the setup code when it finishes. It is also in `journalctl -u msp-atlas`. **Choosing a version:** `--version v1.0.2` installs that release. `sudo bash install-atlas.sh --help` lists every option. **HTTPS:** for a public DNS name, Caddy gets and renews a certificate by itself. For an IP address or a one-word name, it acts as its own certificate authority, which browsers don't trust until you install it. **Admin → Certificate** gives you the file. See [The certificate](manual/looking-after-atlas.html#the-certificate). **Where things go:** the program in `/opt/msp-atlas`, data and backups in `/var/lib/msp-atlas`, settings (`atlas.env`) and the master key in `/etc/msp-atlas`. **Upgrading:** from **Admin → Updates** in Atlas, or run `sudo atlas-install` on the server. Settings, key and database are kept.

Point a DNS name at the server, and open ports 80 and 443. Caddy uses them to get and renew the certificate. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `PUBLIC_URL`, `ATLAS_DOMAIN`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and `ATLAS_MASTER_KEY`. Generate the key with: Start Atlas and read the setup code from the log: A ready-built image is published for each release: `ghcr.io/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas:2.2.0`.

Install Node.js 22 or 24 LTS and PostgreSQL 16 or 17, and create an empty database and user for Atlas. Download `msp-atlas-2.2.0-windows.zip` from the [latest release](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/releases/latest), check it against the `.sha256` file beside it, and extract it to a folder such as `C:\Program Files\MSP Atlas`. From an elevated PowerShell prompt, run: The script creates `C:\ProgramData\MSP Atlas` (readable only by Administrators and SYSTEM), creates the master key file on first install, and registers the `MSPAtlas` service to start automatically. The setup code is in `C:\ProgramData\MSP Atlas\logs\MSPAtlas.out.log`. Atlas listens on `127.0.0.1:4318`. Publish it over HTTPS with IIS (URL Rewrite and Application Request Routing) or Caddy for Windows. Add `-BackupDir \\nas\atlas-backups` to keep backups on another machine. To upgrade, extract the new package over the old folder and run the script again with no arguments. It keeps your settings and key.

The master key protects every encrypted value: vault passwords, one-time code keys, MFA secrets, and the email, Hudu, ConnectWise and SIEM credentials. It also encrypts backups. If you lose the key, encrypted data and backups can't be recovered. Keep a copy in your existing password manager and a sealed printout, never next to database backups. To rotate it, list the new key first and the old one after it, restart, run `npm run rewrap-keys -w @atlas/server`, then remove the old key. Keep the old key for as long as you keep backups made with it.

**Create the owner account.** Open Atlas, enter the setup code, and fill in your company and your own account. **Turn on two-step verification** when asked, and save the recovery codes somewhere other than Atlas. **Back up the master key** as described above. **Set up email** under **Admin → Email & alerts**, and choose **Send test**. Email is needed for password resets, expiry alerts and the weekly digest. **Bring your data in** from Hudu or spreadsheets under **Admin → Import & export**, or connect ConnectWise RMM. See [Data and integrations](manual/integrations.html). **Invite your team** and set their client access under **Admin → People & access**. See [People and access](manual/people-and-access.html). **Check System status** and make sure every check is green. **Admin → Set up Atlas** keeps track of these steps for you. Each one ticks itself off when it's really done (an email server saved, a client added, a backup taken), however you did it, and links straight to where it's done. Until the essential steps are finished, your dashboard shows a **Set up Atlas** card with the next ones.

[People and access](manual/people-and-access.html) for roles, groups and single sign-on. [Keeping Atlas healthy](manual/looking-after-atlas.html) for backups, updates, services and the certificate. The [deployment guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md) lists every setting.

**Admin → People & access** lists everyone who can sign in, with their role, their access, whether two-step verification is on, and when they last signed in. Choose **Manage** to change someone. Add a person Choose **Add person**. Enter their **Name** and **Email**. Choose their **Role**. See [the roles table](getting-started.html#what-you-can-do-depends-on-your-role). Under **Client access**, choose a level for **Every client (including new ones)**, then raise it for individual clients if you need to. Choose **Create account**. Atlas shows a temporary password for them to change at first sign-in. Staff must set up two-step verification before they can do anything else. Access levels For each client, a person has one of **No access**, **Read**, **Edit** or **Edit + passwords**. The **Every client** level applies to every client, including clients added later. A per-client level can raise it for one client. A person's access is the highest of their own levels and their groups' levels, but never more than their role allows. Changes apply straight away, even to people who are signed in. When someone loses their phone Choose **Manage**, then **Reset sign-in**, and tick **Also reset two-step verification**. They set it up again next time they sign in. When someone leaves Edit them and tick **Disable this account**. Their sessions end at once, the browser extension and Atlas for Windows are signed out, and their history stays. Ask them first to move anything in their personal vault that the company needs. **Sign out everywhere** ends every session for a person without disabling them, for example if a laptop is lost. Safeguards You can't change your own role or disable yourself. Administrators can't create, change or reset owners. At least one active owner must remain. Changing someone's role lowers their client access to what the new role allows.

**Admin → Groups** gives a team access to a set of clients in one place. Add people to a group and give the group a level for each client. Someone in several groups gets the highest level any of them gives. Groups can also be listed on restricted passwords.

Staff can sign in with **Microsoft Entra ID** or any **SAML 2.0** identity provider (Okta, Google Workspace, Duo, JumpCloud and others). Both are set up under **Admin → Sign-in**, and both follow the same rules: **Signing in never creates an account.** Add the person in Atlas first, with the same email address they have at the provider. **An administrator confirms each person's first link.** The first time someone signs in, Atlas matches them by email and stops. Open them under **People & access → Manage**, check the name, email and ID shown, and choose **Confirm Microsoft account** or **Confirm SAML account**. After that Atlas recognizes them by the provider's own ID, so a changed address still works and a look-alike address gets nowhere. **The owner can always use a password.** With **Require single sign-on for staff** on, other staff can't sign in with a password or passkey, but the owner can, so a problem at the provider never locks everyone out. **Atlas's own two-step verification still applies** unless you choose to trust the provider's. Microsoft Entra ID In the Microsoft Entra admin center, under **App registrations**, make a separate app for sign-in, and add the **Web** redirect address shown on the **Microsoft sign-in** card. Create a client secret and copy its **Value**. In Atlas, enter the **Sign-in tenant ID**, **Sign-in app ID** and **Sign-in secret**. Tick **Show “Sign in with Microsoft” on the sign-in page** and choose **Save Microsoft sign-in**. Try it in a private window before you tick **Require Microsoft sign-in for staff**. **Trust Microsoft's multi-factor sign-in** skips the Atlas code when Microsoft already asked for more than a password (through conditional access or Security Defaults). SAML In your identity provider, add a SAML app using the **Single sign-on (ACS) URL** and **Audience (SP entity ID)** shown on the **SAML sign-in** card. Send the person's email as an attribute named `email`, and choose a name ID that never changes for a person. The provider must sign the assertion. In Atlas, enter the **Identity provider name** (it goes on the button), its **Provider issuer (entity ID)**, its **Provider sign-on URL**, and paste its **Provider signing certificate**. Tick **Show “Sign in with your provider” on the sign-in page**, choose **Save SAML sign-in**, and try it in a private window before requiring it. Start from the Atlas sign-in page, not the provider's app tile: Atlas refuses a response it didn't ask for. When the provider issues a new certificate, paste the old and new together, then remove the old one once the provider has switched.

**Admin → Vault policies** holds the rules for the whole vault. Every administrator can see them; only the owner can change them. **MFA** Lists every active account that can reach passwords without two-step verification, such as client accounts. **Generator** The shortest password the generator makes, whether it always includes numbers or symbols, and whether it offers PINs. **Require a reason for every reveal, copy, and share** Applies to every client, on top of each client's own setting. **Don't let read-only accounts reveal passwords** Client viewers still see which passwords are shared with them, but can't reveal or copy them. **Restricted passwords are for the people listed on them** Administrators need a place on an entry's list like everyone else. The owner always has access. **Give each staff member a personal vault** Turns My vault on or off for everyone. Turning it off hides the vaults without deleting anything. Emergency access For when the owner can't be reached and a restricted password is needed. The owner adds trusted administrators under **Emergency access**, each with a wait between one hour and a week. A trusted administrator requests access and says why. The owner is emailed at once. During the wait the owner can **Deny** it or **Approve now**. Otherwise access starts when the wait ends, and everyone involved is emailed. Access covers every restricted password for 24 hours. The owner can end it early. Every step is in the security log, and each password used this way says *Emergency access* in its access history. Streaming logs to a SIEM **Stream logs to a SIEM** sends new security events and password access as they happen, about every 30 seconds, by HTTPS webhook (JSON, optionally signed with HMAC-SHA256) or syslog (RFC 5424 over TLS, TCP or UDP). If the SIEM can't be reached, Atlas records the error on the page and tries again from the same place, so nothing is skipped. **Send a test event** checks the connection.

**Admin → Security log** records sign-ins, failures, lockouts, account and access changes, API key use, exports, backups, service actions and updates, each with the address it came from. **Vault access** lists every password reveal, copy, change and share. **Export** either log as CSV. Atlas asks for your password again first. **Verify now** checks that no event has been changed, reordered or removed since it was written. Events are chained together by the database, with a signed checkpoint. Logs are kept forever by default. Choose 1 to 7 years under **Admin → Email & alerts → Alerts and logs**. Someone changed the database directly. Keep the server as it is, export the security log, and investigate. Restore from a backup if you need to.

Atlas sends password reset links, expiry alerts and a Monday digest. Tick **Send email from Atlas**, then choose a mail service. Microsoft 365 (app registration), recommended Atlas signs in as an app registration and sends through Microsoft Graph. No mailbox password or SMTP sign-in is involved. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open **App registrations → New registration** (single tenant, no redirect address). Under **API permissions**, add **Microsoft Graph → Application permissions → Mail.Send**, then **Grant admin consent**. Under **Certificates & secrets**, create a client secret and copy its value. Note when it expires. In Atlas, enter the **Directory (tenant) ID**, **Application (client) ID** and **Client secret**, then the **From address** and **From name**. Choose **Save**, then **Send test**. An Exchange Online application access policy, or RBAC for Applications, can limit the app to the From mailbox so it can't send as anyone else. Other mail services **Microsoft 365 SMTP (legacy)** fills in Office 365's server and port. Microsoft is retiring basic authentication for SMTP, so prefer the app registration. **Other SMTP server** takes an **SMTP server**, **Port**, **Encryption**, **Username** and **Password**. **Send test** shows the mail server's own error if something is wrong. Alerts and logs **Email an alert this many days before something is due.** For example, 30, 14 and 7 days. **Send a weekly digest on Monday mornings,** listing everything overdue or due in the coming weeks. **Keep security and password logs for** a number of years, or forever (the default). People choose whether they receive alerts with **Email me about expirations** on their own account page.

**RMM health** **Stale after (days)** and **Very stale after (days)**: when an agent that hasn't checked in counts as stale. **Asset warranty** **Expiring soon within (days)**, and **Look up warranties automatically** for Dell, Lenovo and HP. **Asset statistics** Which asset layouts count as servers, workstations and other devices. **Domain and SSL trackers** **Check on a schedule** (domains weekly, daily within 60 days of expiry; certificates daily), and **Add SSL certificates for domains**.
Single sign-on with Microsoft Entra ID and SAML is described in [People and access](people-and-access.html#single-sign-on).

API keys let your RMM, PSA or scripts read and update Atlas through its REST API. Choose **New key**. Atlas asks for your password again. Give it a **Name**, choose its scopes (`read`, `write`, and optionally `passwords`), and when it **Expires** (a year unless you choose otherwise). Copy the key. It's shown once; Atlas keeps only a hash of it. **The key acts as you,** with your access, limited to its scopes. Keys can only reach documentation and vault endpoints, never accounts, people, settings, backups or logs. Every use is in the security log. **Revoke** keys you no longer use. The API is at `/api/v1` on your Atlas, described at `/api/v1/openapi.json`. Within v1, updates only add to it, so your scripts keep working. The other `/api` addresses are the web app's own and can change in any release.

**Admin → Theme** sets the **Brand name**, **Tagline**, **Browser tab title**, **Favicon**, a **Logo** (and one for dark mode), the **Accent** colour (and one for dark mode), and the **Welcome message** client accounts see on their dashboard. Text on the accent switches between light and dark to stay readable. Changes preview as you make them, and apply for everyone once you save. Atlas for Windows uses the favicon as its icon too, in its window, the taskbar, the tray, and the Start menu, and picks up a new one within six hours (or when it next starts).

**Admin → Webhooks** makes Atlas post a short message to an address of yours whenever something changes, so a chat channel, an automation or another tool can react. Choose **New webhook**, give it a name and an `https://` address, and tick the kinds of item it should hear about: clients, assets, documents, passwords, contacts, locations, checklists. Copy the **signing secret**, shown once. The receiver uses it to check a message came from Atlas. Choose **Send test** to post a `ping`. A message names the event (such as `asset.updated` or `password.rotated`), who did it, the client, and the item's name and address. It never carries the item's contents, and a password message gives only the entry's name. **Delivery.** Anything other than a 2xx answer within 10 seconds is a failure, tried again after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 6 hours. After ten messages in a row have been given up on, the webhook is paused; fix the receiver and choose **Resume**. **Deliveries** shows the latest 50 and why any failed. An RMM sync changes many assets at once, and each change is a message. Leave **Assets** unticked on a webhook that posts to a chat channel. The signature format and headers are in the [administrator guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/ADMIN-GUIDE.md#webhooks).

Under **Administration → Microsoft Teams**, connect a Microsoft work account for discussions and automatic notifications. No Azure Bot resource or Teams app installation is required. Map each client to its own channel, with an optional separate security destination. Staff open **More → Teams** in a client workspace to read posts and replies, start a discussion, or edit messages they created through Atlas. Alerts cover expirations, document reviews, password breaches and confirmed infection events. Expirations and reviews arrive as a daily digest at reminder milestones; security events are checked every minute. Configure the time zone and alert types, use **Send test notification** after saving, and check **Delivery history** if a message does not arrive. Password values and recovery keys are never posted. See the [Teams setup guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/TEAMS.md) for Microsoft registration, account permissions, reconnection, and the infection-event feed. Alerts appear under the connected account and stay queued if Microsoft requires sign-in again.

In Hudu, go to **Admin → API Keys** and create a key. A key without password access imports everything except passwords. In Atlas, open **Import & export → Hudu**, enter the Hudu address (https only) and the key, and choose **Connect**. The key is encrypted with the master key. Choose what to bring in: kinds of data, companies, and asset layouts. The choices are saved for next time. **Preview** counts what Hudu has. **Start import** runs it in the background, with progress and a summary per type. Companies Clients. A company is matched to an existing client with the same name. Asset layouts and assets Layouts and assets under the matching client. Knowledge base articles Documents for the client, or the MSP knowledge base. Passwords The client's vault, including one-time code keys. Processes Checklists. Networks Networks assets. Relations Links between the imported items. **Running it again is safe.** Atlas remembers which Hudu item became which record and updates it rather than creating a duplicate. Archived Hudu items are skipped.

**Import & export → CSV** brings in clients, contacts, locations, assets (into a chosen layout) or passwords. Choose the kind of data and the file (comma, semicolon or tab separated, up to 10 MB, with a header row). Check the column matching. Atlas matches columns by name, including common alternatives such as "Company", and any column can be reassigned. Choose **Check the file first**.
