It reports every problem with its row number and saves nothing. Choose **Import**. Importing passwords needs **Edit + passwords** on each client involved, and is recorded in the security log.

Atlas reads devices, their health and tickets from the ConnectWise platform API. In ConnectWise RMM, open **Integrations → API Access** and create a client ID and secret. Add the tickets read permission for tickets, and **Automation read** and **Automation create** if you'll use password rotation. In Atlas, enter them under **Import & export → ConnectWise RMM**. Link each ConnectWise company to a client, or let Atlas create the client. Choose what to sync: devices, tickets, and optionally BitLocker keys, by site or device. The sync runs every hour, and **Sync now** runs it straight away. **Devices** become device assets with manufacturer, model, serial number, operating system, last check-in, online status and endpoint protection. Fields you add yourself are kept on each sync. A device the RMM no longer has is archived. **Tickets** are read-only and feed the Tickets cards. **Warranty dates** for Dell, Lenovo and HP are looked up when ConnectWise has none. **BitLocker keys** in a device custom field are saved to the client's vault, linked to the device.

**Import & export → Microsoft 365** documents each client's tenant from one multi-tenant app registration with `Directory.Read.All`, consented once per tenant. Users become contacts (with their licences and admin roles), paid subscriptions become License assets with seats bought and assigned, custom domains become Domain assets, and a Microsoft 365 asset lists the tenant's domains, subscriptions and administrators. For **GDAP**, choose **GDAP — sign in with a partner Microsoft account**, save the partner tenant and multitenant app, and connect the partner account. Add Microsoft Graph delegated **Directory.Read.All**, **DelegatedAdminRelationship.Read.All**, and **LicenseAssignment.ReadWrite.All** permissions, then grant administrator consent. Each customer also needs delegated application consent and an active GDAP relationship with suitable roles assigned to the partner user's security group. Load customers and map each tenant to its Atlas client. **Clients → a client → Licenses** reads Microsoft subscriptions and user assignments through that GDAP connection. Direct assignment/removal requires an Atlas administrator with recent authentication and a supported Microsoft customer role such as **License Administrator** through GDAP. Existing partner connections must reconnect and grant the additional license permission before making license changes. Atlas refuses an application-credential fallback when GDAP fails. Group-derived licenses remain managed through Microsoft Entra group membership; purchasing subscriptions and changing reseller billing terms remain with the reseller. Failed or unconfirmed requests are recorded in the security log; refresh before retrying an uncertain change.

Atlas reads each client's endpoint protection from Bitdefender GravityZone. It's read-only: Atlas never changes anything in GravityZone. In GravityZone, open **My account → API keys** and create a key with the **Network** and **Companies** APIs turned on. A service API key (**Accounts → Service API keys**) works too. Copy the **Access URL** from **My account → Control Center API**. It's usually `https://cloud.gravityzone.bitdefender.com/api`. In Atlas, enter both under **Import & export → Bitdefender GravityZone** and choose **Connect**. Atlas tries the key before saving it, and keeps it encrypted. Link each GravityZone company to a client. A company's name is matched to a client's to suggest the link. The sync runs every hour, and **Sync now** runs it straight away. **The client's overview** gets a **Bitdefender** card. It counts endpoints that are infected, need attention or are protected, and lists what needs attention first, with the reason. It also lists **devices without Bitdefender**: devices the RMM knows about that GravityZone doesn't manage, so they're likely unprotected. **Each device** matched to a GravityZone endpoint shows its state: policy, licence, last seen, agent version, risk score, signatures, and which modules are on. **Needs attention** means the licence has expired or isn't active, the malware signatures are out of date, the policy isn't applied, the endpoint is isolated, it hasn't been seen for 7 days, malware was removed in the last day, or the agent is out of date. **Matching:** endpoints are matched to the client's assets by name, host name or MAC address. Turn on **Add endpoints that aren't in Atlas as assets** to add the rest, in the same layout ConnectWise RMM uses. **Disconnecting** deletes the key and the synced endpoint states. Assets stay.

**One client:** **Export** on the client's page. See [Clients](clients.html#export-a-client). **Everything:** System status → **Back up now** makes a full encrypted backup. See [Keeping Atlas healthy](looking-after-atlas.html#backups). **The API:** with an API key, `/api/v1/openapi.json` describes every endpoint.

**Vault → BitLocker collector** gives you a script for your RMM that reads each Windows machine's BitLocker status and recovery keys and sends them to Atlas. **Make an enrollment.** Choose the client, a name, and whether it covers all of the client's devices or one. The script downloads at once. Keep the file as you would a password: it holds an upload token, and Atlas can't show it again. **Add it to your RMM** as a PowerShell script for that client, run as **SYSTEM**. It needs no parameters. **Try it on one machine.** It prints one line of counts (never keys) and exits 0 when the report was uploaded. **Schedule it** every 6 hours, and after a recovery key is rotated. Machines are matched to assets by serial number, then by name. **Revoke** an enrollment, or **Block** one machine, to stop uploads; keys already saved stay in the vault. The script only reads: it can't turn BitLocker on or off or change a key.

**Vault → Password rotation** changes local administrator and Active Directory service account passwords on a schedule, through ConnectWise RMM. Connect ConnectWise RMM, with **Automation read** and **Automation create** on its API key. Import `deploy/rmm/Invoke-AtlasPasswordRotation.ps1` into ConnectWise RMM as a PowerShell script, enter its ID on the page, and tick **Rotate passwords automatically**. Add a policy for each account type: how often, and the password rules. A policy for **All clients** is the default; a client's own policy replaces it. Choose the passwords: the client, the vault entry, and the device the script runs on. For an AD service account, choose a domain controller. **How it stays safe.** The script sends the new password to Atlas before changing anything, using a token good for that one rotation for two hours. Only a confirmed change replaces the password in the vault; the old one moves to its history. A failure keeps the old password, is recorded in the access history and security log, emails administrators, and is tried again after a day.

Open **Admin → System status** every week or so. It lists anything that needs attention, and shows: **Backups:** the last good backup, the next one, and the history. A red row means the last backup failed, with the reason. **Disk space** for the data and backup folders. **Email**, and the **master key** in use, including whether an old key is still loaded after a rotation. Then open **Security log** and choose **Verify now** to check that no event has been changed or removed.

Atlas backs itself up every night into one encrypted `.atlasbak` file holding the whole database and every attachment, and keeps the newest 14. **Back up now** on System status makes one on demand. **Download** saves a copy; Atlas asks for your password first. Backups are encrypted with a key derived from the master key. Without it, a backup can't be read. System status warns while backups sit on the same disk as Atlas. Point `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR` at a network share, or copy the folder off the server on a schedule. Restore a backup Stop Atlas. Make sure the master key the backup was made with is loaded. Run the restore against a new, empty database, or add `--replace` to overwrite the current one: Start Atlas. Everyone signs in again. The restore checks the whole file before it changes anything. A backup from an older version is upgraded as it loads, and **Verify now** still passes afterwards.

**Admin → Updates** lists the published releases newer than yours, with their release notes. On servers set up with the Linux installer, an administrator can install one from the page: Atlas asks for your password, takes a backup, installs the release, and puts the previous version back if the install fails. Database changes are not rolled back; the pre-update backup covers that. Docker and Windows installs see the page read-only, and update the way they were installed. See [Installing Atlas](../install.html).

**Admin → Services** shows Atlas, the web proxy, the database and the updater, whether each is running, and since when. It works on servers set up with the Linux installer. **Restart** one service. Restarting Atlas takes a few seconds and signs nobody out. Restarting the web proxy drops connections for a moment. Restarting the database restarts Atlas with it. **Repair** is for when something won't start, or can't read or write its files. It puts the owners and permissions of Atlas's settings, master key, program and data folders back as the installer set them, turns the services back on at startup, restarts them, and checks that Atlas answers. It doesn't change your settings, data or version. Every action asks for your password and is written to the security log. If Atlas itself is down, run `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas` on the server, and `sudo journalctl -u msp-atlas -n 50` to see why it stopped.

**Admin → Remote access** chooses how people reach Atlas: from this server directly, through a **Cloudflare Tunnel**, through **Tailscale** (your tailnet, or the internet with Funnel), or behind **your own reverse proxy**. The page lists what to set up first for each, such as the tunnel's public hostname or turning on HTTPS certificates in Tailscale. Choose the way, and fill in the address and the token, auth key or proxy addresses it asks for. Choose **Review the change**. The dialog lists what moves with the address. Choose **Change it**. Atlas restarts on the new address; open it there. Only the owner can change it, after confirming their password. If Atlas doesn't answer at the new address, the server puts the previous settings back. Everyone signs in again. Passkeys only work at the address they were added on, so people add them again. Microsoft and SAML sign-in, the browser extension and Atlas for Windows need the new address.

**Admin → Certificate** shows the certificate Atlas is served with, checked the way a visitor's computer sees it. **Trusted everywhere:** a public authority issued it, because Atlas has a public DNS name. Nothing to do. **Not trusted until installed:** Atlas was installed at an IP address or a one-word name, so the web proxy is its own certificate authority. The connection is encrypted, but browsers warn and Atlas for Windows refuses to connect until that authority is installed on the computer. To install the authority: Choose **Download**. It's a public certificate, not a key. Check its thumbprint against the one on the page, with the PowerShell command the page gives. Install it for the whole computer (as an administrator) or for yourself, with the commands on the page, or push it with Group Policy. Open Atlas at the address on the certificate. A certificate for an IP address doesn't cover a name that points to the same server. A computer that trusts this authority accepts any certificate it issues. Its key is on your Atlas server and only used for Atlas, but install it only on computers you manage. A public DNS name with a public certificate avoids the question.

I lost the setup code With Docker: `docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml logs app | grep "setup code"`. With the Linux installer: `journalctl -u msp-atlas`. On Windows: `C:\ProgramData\MSP Atlas\logs\MSPAtlas.out.log`. It only works until the first account exists. Someone is locked out after too many attempts Wait 15 minutes, or an administrator can use **Reset sign-in** on their account. Someone lost their phone An administrator uses **Reset sign-in** and ticks **Also reset two-step verification**. If the owner lost their phone and recovery codes, another owner or administrator can do it; if there's none, whoever runs the server must help. Sign in with Microsoft or SAML says to wait The first sign-in waits for an administrator to confirm the link under **People & access → Manage**.

A technician can't see a client A client someone can't access looks exactly like a missing one. Check their access for that client, their groups and their role under **People & access**. A password shows but can't be revealed Revealing needs **Edit + passwords** for the client, a place on the entry's list if it's restricted, and a reason if the client requires one.
Email isn't sending **Admin → Email & alerts → Send test** shows the mail server's error. Prefer **Microsoft 365 (app registration)**; for legacy SMTP, Authenticated SMTP must be on for the mailbox.

Backups are failing, or on the same disk Read the error on **System status**. Check the backup folder exists, Atlas can write to it, and the disk isn't full. Point `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR` at a network share to clear the same-disk warning. A restore fails with a key error A backup can only be read with the master key it was made with. After a rotation, list the old key after the new one and try again. Atlas says it can't read or write a file, or a service is stopped **Admin → Services**: restart the service, or use **Repair**. If you can't reach Atlas at all, run `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas` on the server. Browsers warn about the certificate **Admin → Certificate**: download the authority, install it, and open Atlas at the address on the certificate. Verify now reports a break in the security log Someone changed the database directly. Keep the server as it is, export the security log, and investigate. Restore from a backup if needed.

A Hudu import stopped partway Run it again. It updates what it already brought in rather than duplicating it. Duplicates can be merged under **Admin → Duplicates**. ConnectWise devices or tickets are missing Under **Import & export → ConnectWise RMM**, check the company is linked to a client, that devices and tickets are ticked, and read the last sync's messages. Tickets need the tickets read permission. Choose **Sync now** after a change. A warranty date is missing Lookups cover Dell, Lenovo and HP devices with a serial number. Choose **Check warranty** on the asset, or type the date in. A domain or certificate shows as unknown Choose **Check now** on the client's tracker tab. Some registries don't publish an expiry date, and a certificate can only be read from a site Atlas reaches on port 443. Enter the date on the asset for those. A password rotation failed The old password is still in the vault. Read the reason under **Password rotation → Recent attempts**. Check the script ID, that the device is online, and that the API key has Automation read and create.

The browser extension won't sign in Enter your Atlas address, then approve the browser in Atlas after checking the codes match. Its session ends after 7 days unused, 30 days in all, or when your password changes. Atlas for Windows won't connect It refuses a certificate Windows doesn't trust. Install the certificate authority (above) and use the address on the certificate.

Open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/issues) for a verified defect. Never include passwords, master keys, API keys, client data, or screenshots with secrets in them. Report suspected vulnerabilities privately, as described in the [security model](security.html#reporting-a-vulnerability).

**Host and Origin** must match `PUBLIC_URL`; cross-site requests are refused. **The session cookie** (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict) resolves to an active session, and every change carries its CSRF token. **Sign-in is complete:** password, then two-step verification (required for staff), then any required password change. **Client access** (the highest of the person's levels and groups, capped by their role) allows the action. **Passwords** also need edit-and-passwords access, a place on the restriction list, and a reason where required. The reveal is recorded. API keys replace the session with a hashed key limited to its scopes. The extension and Atlas for Windows sign in through the browser and get their own sessions.

Stolen database or backup Secrets are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under keys wrapped by a master key that is never in the database. Backups are encrypted too. Password guessing scrypt hashes, lockout after 5 failures, rate limits, MFA for staff, and passkeys that can't be phished. Stolen session Sessions expire after 2 hours idle or 12 hours; people can end their sessions; sensitive actions ask for the password again. Cross-site attacks Host, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site checks, a CSRF token, and a strict Content Security Policy. Over-broad access inside the MSP Per-client access, restricted passwords, required reasons, and a record of every reveal, copy, change and share. Malicious uploads Stored outside the web root under random names; only images that pass a content check display inline. Tampering with the audit trail Events are hash-chained by the database with a signed checkpoint; **Verify now** detects edits and deletions. Leaked API key Stored as a hash, limited by scope, kept away from account, settings, backup and log endpoints, and can expire. Share links and Send Encrypted in the browser; the key is only in the link's `#` part, which the server never receives. Extension or Windows app on a lost device Neither stores passwords. Both are signed out by a password change or an administrator, and every fill or copy is recorded. An administrator reading restricted passwords Vault policies can limit restricted entries to the people listed. Emergency access is time-limited and emails the owner. Logs can stream to a SIEM. A rotated password that didn't take The vault changes only after the device confirms. Each run uses a single-use token; failures keep the old password.

Atlas is not end-to-end encrypted like a personal password manager. It records every read instead, and lets you restrict entries to named people. Someone who has both the master key and the database. A compromised server, administrator account, or signed-in person's device. Server-side requests an administrator sets up: the Hudu importer connects to any `https://` address, including internal ones. A compromised ConnectWise account. Password rotation runs scripts through ConnectWise RMM, so whoever controls it already controls those devices.

Serve Atlas only over HTTPS. Keep the master key in a password manager and on paper, not next to backups. Keep backups off the Atlas server, and check them with `npm run backup -w @atlas/server -- verify `. Check **System status** and **Security log → Verify now** regularly.

Never in a public issue. Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting (**Security → Report a vulnerability**) with the affected version, impact and steps to reproduce. See the [security policy](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

**Check that last night's backup finished.** It's under **Administration → System status**. If backups sit on the same disk as Atlas, copy the newest one somewhere else. **Make sure you can lay your hands on the master key** (`/etc/msp-atlas/master.key` on Linux, or wherever you keep your copy). A backup can't be restored without it. **Pick a quiet time.** Atlas restarts while it updates, and is usually back within a few minutes.

**Installed with the Linux installer:** go to **Administration → Updates** and choose **Install** on 2.0. Atlas asks for your password and takes a backup before anything changes. It then installs the release and restarts. If the install fails, it puts the previous version back on its own. From a terminal, `sudo atlas-install --version v2.0.0` does the same. **Docker:** pull the 2.0 image and run `docker compose ... up -d`, after a backup. **Windows Server:** run the 2.0 package's `Install-Atlas.ps1`, after a backup. Atlas updates its database the first time 2.0 starts. Nothing needs doing by hand.

Everyone sees a **Welcome to Atlas 2.0** card on their dashboard. It leads to the What's new page, which is always under **What's new** in the account menu. In short: **Reports:** a client review pack; reports that email themselves on a schedule, and alerts that only send when something new needs attention; a cyber insurance readiness report; a savings finder; Microsoft 365 accounts and usage; every report readable on one page. **A health score for every client.** **Faster documenting:** smart paste for assets, Wi-Fi join codes, and the Licenses page showing everything at once. **A cleaner workspace.** Your menu style (rail and panel, sidebar, or top bar) carries over. **Atlas for Windows 1.0.**

**The Monthly report button** on a client's page. The client's **Reports** tab replaces it, with PDFs, share links and schedules, and old links to the monthly report open that tab. **The 0.2 importer.** If you still have an Atlas 0.2 database, move it with Atlas 1.8 before upgrading. **Scripts:** the supported API is `/api/v1`. API keys only ever worked there, so nothing you've set up changes.

These take a few minutes, and only the ones that apply to you matter. Everyone **Look at the dashboard's Set up Atlas card** (administrators). It lists anything an installation should have and doesn't yet, such as email or a recent backup. If you use Microsoft 365 with GDAP The new **Microsoft 365 usage** report reads Microsoft's usage reports, which need a permission Atlas didn't ask for before. In your partner app registration, add the Microsoft Graph delegated permission **Reports.Read.All** and grant consent. Give your GDAP security group a role that can read usage reports, such as **Reports Reader**. In Atlas, under **Administration → Import & export → Microsoft 365**, choose **Reconnect partner account**. Everything else carries on as before. Until you do this, the usage report says what's missing rather than failing quietly. See [Data and integrations](integrations.html). If you send reports or alerts by email Scheduled reports and alerts are sent through the email server under **Administration → Email & alerts**. Choose **Send test** there to make sure it works. If your favicon is an SVG Atlas for Windows uses your favicon as its icon, and Windows can't draw an SVG. Open **Administration → Theme** and choose **Save** once: Atlas makes a picture Windows can use. Atlas for Windows Technicians' copies offer **Install and restart** for version 1.0 on their own, within six hours, or straight away from **Check for updates**. New installs download it from **Your account → Desktop apps**. One download works on every PC, including Arm laptops. If your organization hasn't set up code signing, Windows SmartScreen still asks before the setup program runs: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**.

If something important doesn't work, you can return to the version you had. The backup taken before the upgrade holds everything as it was. On Linux (installed with the installer): Install the previous release, for example `sudo atlas-install --version v1.8.4`. Stop Atlas: `sudo systemctl stop msp-atlas`. Restore the backup taken just before the upgrade. It's the newest file in the backups folder (`/var/lib/msp-atlas/backups` unless you changed `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR`) from before you upgraded: ```bash cd /opt/msp-atlas sudo runuser -u atlas -- node --env-file=/etc/msp-atlas/atlas.env apps/server/dist/cli/restore.js /var/lib/msp-atlas/backups/.atlasbak --replace ``` Start Atlas: `sudo systemctl start msp-atlas`. Everyone signs in again. Anything changed in Atlas after the upgrade is lost by going back, because the backup is from before it. For Docker and Windows, go back to the previous image or package, then restore the same way (see [Keeping Atlas healthy](looking-after-atlas.html#restore-a-backup)). If you go back, please say what didn't work through the support channel or GitHub, so it can be fixed in 2.0.1.
